Text.name: scope_rule_text
Text.value: Annotate the current space containing the camera. Follow its enclosing walls through corners that belong to the current space. When an opening leads to an adjacent space, close the layout at a clear structural boundary—such as a door frame, paired wall returns or jambs, or an arch—and do not continue into the adjacent space. Choose In-scope whenever this space has one reproducible single-level Manhattan wall–ceiling–floor enclosure. Local occlusion, an opening, stairs, or a ceiling recess is not automatically OOS. Choose OOS only when a specific reason below applies.

Choices.name: scope
Choices.requiredMessage: Scope is required. Select exactly one option.

Choice.value: In-scope: current space containing the camera
Choice.hint: Follow the enclosing walls through ordinary L/T-shaped corners that belong to the current space. When an opening leads to an adjacent space, close at a clear structural boundary such as a door frame, paired wall returns or jambs, or an arch. Choose this whenever the current space has one reproducible single-level Manhattan wall–ceiling–floor enclosure. Local occlusion, openings, or stairs and ceiling recesses that can be excluded at a clear boundary remain in-scope.

Use when the dominant structure of the current space cannot be stably represented by one Manhattan/cuboid-style enclosure. Typical cases include curved walls, continuous curved surfaces, obvious slanted walls, or another dominant non-Manhattan structure. An L/T-shaped Manhattan space is not OOS for this reason.

Choice.value: OOS: open or ambiguous boundary of the current space
Choice.hint: Use when an opening to an adjacent space has no reproducible structural boundary, or when multiple closures are equally plausible. Merely seeing an adjacent space through an opening is not OOS if you can close at a door frame, paired wall returns or jambs, or an arch. If key evidence is missing or invisible, prefer insufficient evidence.

Use when one enclosure for the current space must include competing floor or ceiling levels and cannot satisfy a single-floor and single-ceiling assumption. If stairs or a sunken area can be cleanly excluded at a visible boundary and the current space still closes uniquely, choose in-scope.

Use when key structural evidence is genuinely missing and a reproducible enclosure cannot be determined. Typical causes include severe occlusion, overexposure, blur, missing panorama regions, black borders, or large masks. Do not use this for a local occlusion, one uncertain corner, or an abstract image when the current space still closes stably.

Text.name: difficulty_rule_text
Text.value: Select the factors that materially made the layout or corner annotation harder in this task. Difficulty describes annotation difficulty; it does not determine Scope or indicate whether the model is wrong. Select multiple labels when distinct factors independently increase difficulty, but do not apply multiple labels to the same underlying cause. Select at least one option. Choose trivial only when no other factor materially increases difficulty, and do not combine it with another label.

Choices.name: difficulty
Choices.requiredMessage: Difficulty is required. Select at least one option.

Choice.hint: Choose only when no other factor materially increases layout or corner annotation difficulty. This label is mutually exclusive with every other difficulty label.

A foreground object or structure blocks wall, corner, or boundary evidence that would otherwise need to be judged. An enclosing wall is not an occluder merely because it is visible. If the enclosure can no longer be closed reproducibly, consider insufficient evidence.

The image is complete, but local texture, color, or contrast is too weak, so boundaries or corners rely on subtle geometric cues. Do not apply this label again when the same difficulty already has a clearer occlusion, seam, reflection, or low-quality cause.

Panorama stitching, reprojection, stretching, or local geometric distortion makes true corners hard to locate. This may appear as broken lines, shifted walls, or corner drift; the root cause is seam/stretch distortion.

Mirrors or glass create false boundaries, duplicated structure, or depth confusion that materially increases layout or corner annotation difficulty. Do not select this merely because glass or a mirror is present.

Choice.value: Blur, mask, or low image quality
Choice.hint: Blur, noise, compression artifacts, large masks, black borders, or missing pixels make key wall–floor–ceiling or opening-boundary evidence unreliable. Do not apply this label again when the same difficulty has a clearer local occlusion or seam cause.
